claim: Non-refoulement claim due to risk of torture or death in India
requested_remedy: Non-refoulement claim due to risk of torture or death in India
parties: Defendant: Torture Claims Appeal Board/Non-Refoulement Claims Petition Office and Director of Immigration

facts.F1: The applicant, an Indian national, claimed he would be tortured or killed by his uncle Joginder Singh, a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), due to a dispute over land inheritance.
facts.F2: The applicant's grandfather left land to his sons without a will, leading to a dispute between the applicant's father and Joginder.
facts.F3: Joginder threatened the applicant and caused him physical harm on multiple occasions, leading the applicant to flee India for safety.
facts.F4: The applicant entered Hong Kong on July 25, 2014, as a visitor and overstayed, leading to his arrest by the police on August 13, 2014.
facts.F5: The applicant lodged a non-refoulement claim, which was denied by the Director of Immigration and the Torture Claims Appeal Board/Non-Refoulement Claims Petition Office (TCAB/NCPO).
facts.F6: The applicant applied for judicial review on October 9, 2017.
facts.F7: The Director's decision contained clear findings, conclusions, and decisions.
facts.F8: The Adjudicator considered various country-of-origin information (COI) reports referred to by the immigration officer.
facts.F9: The Director and Adjudicator considered the Applicant's case carefully and applied the law correctly.

lawsuit_type: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review
reference_issues: Whether the Director and Adjudicator failed to consider state acquiescence
Whether there was insufficient inquiry
Whether the decision-makers failed to provide adequate reasons
Whether the decision-makers failed to investigate country-of-origin information (COI) relating to India
Whether the decision-makers selectively placed weight on irrelevant information
Whether the decision-makers failed to consider a consistent system of human rights violations in India
Whether state protection existed in India
authorities:
Hong Kong Bill of Rights (HKBOR)
Unified Screening Mechanism
Part VIIC of the Immigration Ordinance, Cap 115 ("Torture Risk")

claim: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review of the decisions of the Director of Immigration and the Torture Claims Appeal Board
requested_remedy: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review of the decisions of the Director of Immigration and the Torture Claims Appeal Board
parties: Defendant: Director of Immigration and Torture Claims Appeal Board

facts.F1: The applicant entered Hong Kong as a visitor on 13 June 2014 and overstayed until 22 September 2014 when he surrendered to the Immigration Department.
facts.F2: He lodged a claim for non-refoulement protection on 29 October 2014, alleging that he would be harmed or killed by his granduncle and his son over a land dispute if he were to return to India.
facts.F3: The Director of Immigration rejected his claim on 19 January 2016 on the grounds of risk of torture, CIDTP, and persecution with reference to the non-refoulement principle.
facts.F4: The applicant appealed to the Torture Claims Appeal Board, which dismissed his appeal on 23 December 2016.
facts.F5: The Director invited the applicant to submit additional facts relevant to his claim for non-refoulement under the right to life on 15 February 2017.
facts.F6: The applicant filed a second appeal to the Board against the Director's further decision on 13 March 2017, which was dismissed on 25 April 2017.
facts.F7: The applicant filed an application for leave to apply for judicial review of the decisions of the Director and the Board on 9 May 2017.
facts.F8: The applicant was born in Village Taggar Kallan, District Hoshiarpur, Punjab, India, and has been involved in a land dispute with his granduncle Harbhajan Singh (HS).
facts.F9: The applicant alleged that HS and his men attacked him in December 2013, causing him pain and bruises all over his body, and he escaped to his father-in-law's home in District Gurdaspur.
facts.F10: The applicant did not report the assault to the police, but his father-in-law arranged for him to fly to Hong Kong on 13 June 2014.
facts.F11: The applicant received the Director's Further Decision on 7 March 2017.
facts.F12: The applicant had almost six weeks to submit additional facts or materials to the Board before his appeal was dismissed on 25 April 2017.
facts.F13: The applicant alleged that his family was constantly threatened and tortured, his home was burnt, his mother was seriously injured, and his cousin sister died from torture, but failed to produce evidence to support these allegations.

lawsuit_type: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review
reference_issues: Whether the applicant was deprived of the opportunity to submit additional facts relevant to his non-refoulement claim under BOR 2 Risk.

Whether there was procedural unfairness in the consideration of objective COI by the Director and the Board in finding that internal relocation was available and reasonable for the applicant to return to live and work safely in India.

claim: The Applicant sought leave to apply for judicial review of the Torture Claims Appeal Board’s decision to dismiss her appeal against the Director of Immigration’s decision to reject her claim for non-refoulement protection.
requested_remedy: The Applicant sought leave to apply for judicial review of the Torture Claims Appeal Board’s decision to dismiss her appeal against the Director of Immigration’s decision to reject her claim for non-refoulement protection.

facts.F1: The Applicant is a 46-year-old national of Indonesia who arrived in Hong Kong on 23 August 2006 with permission to work as a foreign domestic helper.
facts.F2: Her last contract was prematurely terminated on 8 September 2009, and she did not depart Hong Kong, but overstayed and was arrested by police on 23 October 2009.
facts.F3: She raised a torture claim on the basis that if she returned to Indonesia, she would be harmed or killed by her abusive husband over their monetary dispute.
facts.F4: Her torture claim was rejected, and she then raised a claim for non-refoulement protection on the same basis.
facts.F5: She was subsequently released on recognizance pending the determination of her claim.
facts.F6: The Applicant was born and raised in Desa Purwodadi, Kecamatan Ringin Rejo, Kabupaten Kediri, East Java, Indonesia.
facts.F7: She married her husband, but he was frequently unemployed, and she went to work in Singapore in 1999 as a domestic helper.
facts.F8: She returned to Indonesia in 2002, but her husband beat her during a quarrel.
facts.F9: The Applicant left her marriage and moved to Jakarta, where she worked as a domestic helper, and had no further contact with her husband since 2002.
facts.F10: In 2004, she moved to Batam to work as a restaurant waitress before coming to Hong Kong in 2006 to work as a foreign domestic helper.
facts.F11: When her last employment contract was prematurely terminated, she did not return to Indonesia due to fear of harm from her husband and overstayed in Hong Kong.
facts.F12: Upon her arrest by the police, she raised her torture claim, and after it was rejected by the Immigration Department, she then sought non-refoulement protection.
facts.F13: The Applicant was arrested by police again in 2010 for the offense of deception and undertaking unauthorized employment, for which she was subsequently convicted on 21 October 2010 and sentenced to prison for 16 months.
facts.F14: The Applicant participated in the screening process and interview before the Immigration Department and in the process before the Board.
facts.F15: The Applicant’s grounds for challenging the Board’s decision were broad and vague, containing several pages of key words and phrases but without any particulars or specifics or elaborations.

reference_issues: Whether the Torture Claims Appeal Board erred in law in dismissing the Applicant’s appeal.
Whether the Board’s decision was procedurally unfair or irrational.

facts.F1: The Applicant, a Gambian national, entered Hong Kong on 20 June 2014 as a visitor until 18 September 2014.
facts.F2: He remained as an over-stayer since 19 September 2014 and surrendered to the Immigration Department on 29 September 2014.
facts.F3: He lodged a non-refoulement protection claim on 23 October 2014, citing fear of harm from his half-brother and step-mother due to a land dispute.
facts.F4: His non-refoulement claims were assessed on three grounds: Torture Risk; BOR 3 Risk; and Persecution Risk.
facts.F5: The Director of Immigration (the Director) rejected his claims on 23 December 2015 (the 2015 Notice).
facts.F6: The Applicant applied for late filing of his notice of appeal/petition to the Board on 22 July 2016, which was refused on 6 February 2017 (the 2017 Decision).

facts.F9: The Applicant petitioned against the 2017 Notice and was dismissed by the Board on 30 November 2018 (the 2018 Decision).
facts.F10: The Applicant applied for leave to apply for judicial review of the 2018 Decision on 10 December 2018.
facts.F11: The court will intervene, by way of judicial review, for errors of law, procedural unfairness or irrationality.

facts.F1: The applicant, a national of Pakistan, came to Hong Kong on 28 November 2016 as a visitor and overstayed since 12 December 2016.
facts.F2: He surrendered to the Immigration Department on 15 December 2016 and lodged a non-refoulement claim by way of written representation dated 19 January 2017.
facts.F3: The applicant claimed that if refouled, he would be harmed or killed by his wife's family because they opposed their matrimonial relationship.
facts.F4: The applicant's wife died after giving birth to twins, and he alleged that her family members were responsible for her death due to ill-treatment and brutality.
facts.F5: The Director considered his application in relation to torture risk under Part VIIC of the Immigration Ordinance, BOR 2 risk, BOR 3 risk, and Persecution risk.

facts.F2: The Applicant claimed he was involved in a business deal with Jaswinder, the Youth President of the Akali Dal Party, but Jaswinder stole the money and returned to India, leaving the Applicant in Hong Kong.
facts.F3: The Applicant reported Jaswinder's theft to the Hong Kong police and later raised a torture claim and non-refoulement claim.

claim: The applicants claimed non-refoulement protection in Hong Kong on the basis that if refouled to Sri Lanka they would be at the same risk of harm as the 1st applicant's husband who had raised a torture claim, and if refouled to Indonesia they would be harmed by the 1st applicant's former fiancé for failing to marry him and by her family for marrying a non-Indonesian man against their wish.
requested_remedy: The applicants claimed non-refoulement protection in Hong Kong on the basis that if refouled to Sri Lanka they would be at the same risk of harm as the 1st applicant's husband who had raised a torture claim, and if refouled to Indonesia they would be harmed by the 1st applicant's former fiancé for failing to marry him and by her family for marrying a non-Indonesian man against their wish.
parties: Plaintiff: The 1st applicant (A1) and The 2nd applicant (A2)

facts.F1: The 1st applicant (A1) is a 43-year-old national of Indonesia who arrived in Hong Kong on 22 January 2002 as a foreign domestic helper and later formed a relationship with a Sri Lankan torture claimant with whom she had a son, the 2nd applicant (A2) born on 24 February 2007 in Hong Kong.
facts.F2: A1's employment contract was prematurely terminated on 15 April 2007, and she overstayed until 23 May 2007 when she surrendered to the Immigration Department.
facts.F3: A1 and her husband lodged a torture claim on the basis that if refouled to Sri Lanka they would be at the same risk of harm as under his claim.
facts.F4: After her husband's torture claim was rejected, A1 and A2 jointly lodged a non-refoulement claim on the same basis, and subsequently A1 proceeded with her claim with additional risk of fear of harm from her former fiancé and family if refouled to Indonesia.
facts.F5: The Director of Immigration rejected their claim on all applicable grounds other than torture claim, and the Torture Claims Appeal Board dismissed their appeal.
facts.F6: The applicants applied for judicial review, but their application was five months late, and they failed to provide valid reasons for the delay.
facts.F7: The court considered the length of the delay, the reasons for the delay, the merits of the intended application, prejudice to the putative respondent, and questions of general public importance when evaluating the applicants' delay in applying for judicial review.
facts.F8: The applicants' application for judicial review was not reasonably arguable.
facts.F9: The Director and the Board's evaluation of the risk of harm was rigorously examined by the court with anxious scrutiny.

facts.F1: The applicant, a Mongolian national, arrived in Hong Kong on a visa but overstayed since 24 February 2018.
facts.F2: The applicant applied for non-refoulement protection on 26 March 2018, claiming he would be harmed or killed by his previous employers if returned to Mongolia due to informing on their alleged criminal activities.
facts.F3: The Director of Immigration considered the applicant's claim under Part VIIC of the Immigration Ordinance (Cap 115) (Torture Risk), Article 2 of Section 8 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance (Cap 383) (BOR 2 Risk), Article 3 of section 8 of the HKBOR (BOR 3 Risk), and the non-refoulement principle under Article 33 of the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol (Refugee Convention).
facts.F4: The Director's Decision (dated 4 October 2018) refused the applicant's claim, citing a lack of substantial grounds to believe in a real risk, availability of state protection, and the option of internal relocation.
facts.F5: The applicant appealed the decision without a hearing, and the Board's Decision (dated 9 November 2018) rejected the appeal, citing unreliable and uncredible evidence, as well as the failure to support the non-refoulement claim.
facts.F6: The Court applied the principle of rigorous examination and anxious scrutiny in reviewing the Board's Decision.
